lesson.title: Inside the Atom: The Building Blocks of Matter
lesson.summary: This section breaks matter down to the atomic scale, explaining protons, neutrons, and electrons, and how atomic number defines identity.
lesson.body:
In the last section you learned that matter is anything with mass that occupies space. Atoms are the fundamental unit that all ordinary matter, whether solid, liquid, or gas, is built from. An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still retains the chemical identity of that element. Atoms are extraordinarily small: roughly one hundred million atoms of carbon lined up in a row would span only about one centimeter. Despite this tiny size, atoms are not indivisible in the way early Greek philosophers imagined when they coined the word atomos, meaning uncuttable. Atoms are themselves made of smaller subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons.

Protons and neutrons cluster together in a dense central region called the nucleus, which accounts for nearly all of an atom's mass despite occupying only a tiny fraction of its volume. Protons carry a positive electric charge, neutrons carry no charge, and together they are held in the nucleus by the strong nuclear force, which overcomes the electrical repulsion between the positively charged protons. Electrons, which carry a negative charge, occupy the much larger space surrounding the nucleus, moving too fast and unpredictably to be pictured as tiny planets on fixed orbits. A more accurate picture, developed later in quantum mechanics, describes regions of space called orbitals where an electron is likely to be found. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons exactly equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges balance and the atom has no overall charge.

The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is called its atomic number, and this single number defines which element the atom is. Every atom with exactly 6 protons is a carbon atom, whether it has 6, 7, or 8 neutrons; every atom with exactly 8 protons is an oxygen atom. Neutrons contribute to an atom's mass without changing its chemical identity, so atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These variants are called isotopes. Carbon 12, with 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and carbon 14, with 6 protons and 8 neutrons, are both carbon, and both behave almost identically in chemical reactions, but carbon 14 is radioactive and used in dating ancient organic material because of its unstable nucleus.

Mass in atoms is measured using the atomic mass unit, defined so that a single proton or neutron has a mass close to 1 amu, while an electron's mass is nearly negligible by comparison, about 1800 times smaller. This is why an atom's mass is essentially determined by its protons and neutrons together, a quantity called the mass number. A helium atom, with 2 protons and 2 neutrons, has a mass number of 4 and an atomic mass close to 4.00 amu. Electrons, despite contributing almost nothing to mass, are what actually control how atoms interact with each other, since it is the outermost electrons, not the protons or neutrons buried in the nucleus, that are exchanged or shared when atoms bond. That electron behavior is exactly what determines the patterns you will see in the next section, when atoms are organized into elements and the periodic table.
